_doc: Cross-cutting concepts the book repeatedly invokes. `definedIn` points to the note where the concept gets its primary development. `coveredBy` lists chapters that discuss it. Card layer (see build-graph.js): `plain` is the one-sentence reader-facing statement; `passages` lists { note, section } H2s where the idea is argued in full (validated); `related` (typed ids) is the curated see-also; `instanceOf` / `derivesFrom` (typed ids) are special-case / builds-on links; `autolink` is false or an explicit list of terms for scripts/interlink.js (default: label + aliases). The reader-facing card body is prose and lives in content/concepts/<id>.md between the <!-- card --> markers.

concepts.label: Receiver budget
concepts.summary: A human has finite time, effective mental hours, and capacity to absorb new information. The constraint is real but not fixed — education, vocabulary, and accumulated structure expand the *capacity* of each hour, even if the hours themselves are fixed. Want is the gate that decides what the budget gets spent on, which is what makes the medium-shapes-want loop a receiver-budget mechanism rather than just a content one. Ch 11's decompression-on-demand is the first structural softening of the per-claim cost the book has been able to name, conditional on faithful LLM substrate custody. Ch 4 (optionality-vs-access) shows the same constraint reflected in artifact design — the optionality-vs-access curve is the receiver-budget constraint refracted into how artifacts have to be designed for their intended audiences.
concepts.plain: Each person has only so many focused hours to learn new things, though what you already know makes every hour go further.

passages.section: Want decides what the budget is spent on

concepts.label: Complexity ceiling
concepts.summary: The maximum complexity an idea can carry across a network is bounded by network size and accumulated selection/transport pressure. Bigger network, lower ceiling.
concepts.plain: The more people an idea has to pass through, the simpler it must become to survive the trip.

concepts.label: Compressed form
concepts.summary: Low-precondition version of an idea. Cheap for receivers to process, plugs into existing mental structures, easy to re-transmit. Free to share, easy to weaponize.
concepts.plain: The short, easy version of an idea spreads fast because it asks almost nothing of the person hearing it.

concepts.label: Complex form
concepts.summary: High-precondition version of an idea. Requires receivers to load preconditions, work through implications, decide whether the new structure fits. Expensive but lossless.
concepts.plain: The full version of an idea keeps what the short version drops, but it only makes sense to someone who already knows a lot.

concepts.label: Manipulation surface
concepts.summary: What attackers can exploit. Grows with network size in the pure-transport view; with tunable selection-gate criteria in the full view. Recommendation algorithms are selection engines with adjustable weights — the more dangerous formulation.
concepts.plain: The most powerful way to steer what a crowd believes is to change the rules deciding what spreads, and that takes no lies.

passages.section: The manipulation surface is the gate itself
Three things the medium does to a gate

concepts.label: Three realities (Harari)
concepts.summary: Objective (independent of observer — atoms, planets, dogs), subjective (in one mind — pains, dreams, qualia), intersubjective (real because enough people agree — currencies, nations, brands, laws, religions). The pipeline operates differently on each: objective claims have a fact-of-the-matter the pipeline either transmits faithfully or distorts (the book's diagnostic vocabulary applies cleanly); subjective claims mostly don't traverse the pipeline; intersubjective realities are partly constituted by the pipeline rather than transmitted through it (so the relevant failure mode is capture of the constitutive process, not truth-loss in transit). Ch 2 makes the distinction explicit to flag where the book's diagnostic vocabulary needs translation between reality types.
concepts.plain: Some things are true whatever anyone thinks, some only inside one mind, and some only because enough people agree, like money or laws.

concepts.label: Bridge zone
concepts.summary: The space between deep specialists and mass audiences. Where journalism, popularizers, influencers, and AI summarizers live. Where selection pressures are most intense and active reshaping happens.
concepts.plain: Most expert knowledge reaches the public through journalists, popularizers, influencers and chatbots, and that handoff is where it gets reshaped the most.

concepts.label: Echo chambers vs. bubbles (Nguyen)
concepts.summary: Epistemic bubbles are missing-info structures; echo chambers actively discredit outside info. Small networks tend toward chambers, which changes what 'infrastructure for integration' has to do.
concepts.plain: Never hearing the other side is one thing; being taught to distrust anyone outside your group is another, and small groups drift toward the second.

concepts.label: Curation layer
concepts.summary: Infrastructure that decouples access from quality assurance — low barriers to enter, robust mechanisms to surface the best work. Wikipedia's editorial apparatus, Stack Overflow reputation. From the democratization-paradox post.
concepts.plain: Let anyone contribute, then use open, layered review to sort the good from the bad, as Wikipedia does.

concepts.label: Cost-shifting from producers to consumers
concepts.summary: When barriers to creation fall, the cost of quality assessment doesn't disappear — it transfers from producers (who used to bear it as the price of being published at all) onto consumers, reviewers, and maintainers, who have no more time than before and no ledger entry for the cost. The structural move that lets the platform political economy stay invisible: the platform claims credit for democratizing access while the actual access-to-quality collapses, because the cost landed on someone with no balance sheet to absorb it.
concepts.plain: When publishing became free, the work of checking what is true did not vanish; it moved onto readers, who have no extra time for it.

concepts.label: Self-capture vs. external capture
concepts.summary: Two flavors of institutional capture at the platform scale, structurally different. External capture: an adversarial selection-tuner (propaganda operation, state actor, ad-tech firm) learns the platform's gate criteria and crafts variants that win at them — the asymmetric arms race shape. Self-capture: the institution's own business model is the captured selection-tuner — engagement maximization is itself a tuning of the gates against truth, with no external adversary. Self-capture is more stable than external capture because there is no captor to defeat, only an equilibrium to dismantle; the captured state and the functional state are the same state. Per the capture-taxonomy these are the two endpoints of the source axis, and the empirically dominant third case is composite capture — external actors riding the gradient self-capture has already established.
concepts.plain: An institution can be bent by outsiders gaming its rules or by its own way of making money, and the second is harder to undo.

passages.section: Axis 2: who is doing the capturing

concepts.label: Out-competition of institutional carriers in attention markets
concepts.summary: Platforms do not have to suppress institutional carriers (journals, universities, depth journalism) to hollow them. Free engagement-optimized content has approximately zero marginal cost of attention because users produce it; depth content has real cost-per-impression because the institutional apparatus is paid. The attention market clears at zero price for engagement-optimized noise and infinite price for depth, so receivers — with limited attention and no quality-assessment budget — predictably pick the free option. The mechanism that produces Ch 8's asymmetric institutional collapse without any direct attack on the institutions.
concepts.plain: Careful journalism and scholarship cost money to make while feed content costs platforms nothing, so depth loses the audience without anyone ever attacking it.

passages.section: Why institutional carriers can't keep up

concepts.label: Inverted-U relationship
concepts.summary: Refines the binary 'small vs. large networks' framing: there's an optimum. Small networks have their own internal compression dynamics; very large networks collapse under selection pressure.
concepts.plain: For things like group size and how connected people are, the best amount sits in the middle, and both too little and too much hurt.

concepts.label: Creation cheap / review expensive
concepts.summary: When content generation scales faster than curation infrastructure, noise wins regardless of how many gems are in the flood. LLMs accelerate the asymmetry on both sides.
concepts.plain: Making content has become far quicker than checking it, so the unchecked pile grows faster than anyone can sort it.

concepts.label: Preservation vs. training (paired institutional functions)
concepts.summary: What 'bureaucracy' was bundling: preservation keeps the un-compressed form alive somewhere; training re-installs the capacity to decode at that resolution in receivers. Each can be done by many institutional forms (monasteries, journals, universities, common-law courts, version-controlled specs) and each fails differently when starved, captured, or displaced. The pair acts as a pump — preservation holds pressure, training releases it into the network — so either alone fails the integration project.
concepts.plain: Keeping hard knowledge alive takes two jobs at once: storing the full original somewhere, and continually teaching people how to read it.

concepts.label: Survival, not victory (integration institutions)
concepts.summary: The prescriptive reframe at the heart of Ch 12. Institutions that succeed at the integration project are institutions that survive being out-competed for attention and still deliver preserve-and-retrain — they do not need to displace the captured equilibrium, they need to operate alongside it without being eroded by it. Survival-design and victory-design produce different institutions: victory-design tries to clear the attention market by being more engaging (and gets captured by the market's selection pressure); survival-design refuses to compete in the attention market and finds funding outside it. The framing matters because almost every modern attempt at integration infrastructure has been victory-designed and has drifted toward engagement-optimization or starved.
concepts.plain: Careful institutions cannot beat the attention economy, so the goal is to keep doing their work alongside it without being worn down.

concepts.label: Funding decoupling from attention markets
concepts.summary: The structural counter to Ch 10's out-competition mechanism. Institutional carriers cannot survive if they have to clear a free-engagement market — they have to compete with platforms' zero-marginal-cost attention and lose. The only survivable funding shapes are those whose revenue is not a function of how well the institution clears the attention market: endowments and patient capital, public funding through credibly neutral allocation, member dues and mission-driven subscriptions, public-goods funding mechanisms (retroactive funding, quadratic funding, crypto-economic public-goods primitives). Revenue contracted in a different market than the engagement-optimization noise lets the institution lose the engagement-market clearing entirely without losing capacity to operate. The first of Ch 12's three load-bearing design principles.
concepts.plain: An institution that does slow, careful work has to be paid in some way that does not depend on winning people's attention.

passages.section: Principle 1: decouple funding from attention markets
Why institutional carriers can't keep up

concepts.label: Survivable polarization (design for partial trust)
concepts.summary: Design principle for integration institutions: build for institutions that work even when trust is partially eroded, not for institutions that require trust to be complete. The polarization-via-distrust trap from Ch 9 means evidence channels get filtered out by communities that distrust the source — so the integration infrastructure has to do its work across trust boundaries that will not be repaired in advance. Properties: decision provenance auditable by skeptics; reputation systems whose underlying signal survives partial distrust in the aggregator; versatile experts inhabiting the institution rather than presiding over it; multiple independent decision pathways for the same question (route around capture, get Zollman-effect accuracy benefits as a bonus). Wikipedia's edit history, common-law jurisdictional variation, replicated lab results are existing partial implementations.
concepts.plain: Build institutions that still work when some people distrust them, by letting doubters check the evidence and reasoning for themselves.

concepts.label: LLM as capability extender (inside substrate custody)
concepts.summary: The Ch 11 salvation case, structurally specified by Ch 12. Faithful LLMs running with institution-owned substrates — corpus, objective, deployment all governed by the institution rather than by a commercial vendor — function as a capability extender for preserve-and-retrain: decompression-on-demand against the institution's preservation archive for trainees, Socratic instruction at scale, drafting and synthesis that versatile experts then verify. Not a replacement for institutional experts but a tool that makes their work go faster and reach more receivers. Requires open weights, transparent corpus custody, credibly neutral objective specification, and institution-controlled deployment — none of which is the default in the commercial LLM landscape. The integration-friendly LLM configuration is technically realizable, economically marginal, and politically blocked by the same forces that captured the social-media equilibrium.
concepts.plain: A university that trains and runs its own AI on its own vetted library could teach far more people, with real experts checking the output.

passages.section: LLMs as a capability extender, conditional on custody

concepts.label: Work of generations (institutional timescale)
concepts.summary: The closing reframe of Ch 12. Institutions of integration are civilization-scale investments on the timescale of universities, journals, common-law systems, and open-source ecosystems — built and drifted on generational timescales, not platform-launch timescales. The captured equilibrium of the platform business model built itself in two decades; the integration institutions that hold against it will need at least that long to be built, and will need to be funded and staffed and politically protected through the building. The prescription is not a recipe for next quarter — it is a brief for the civilization-scale investment that built the institutions the modern environment has been disinvesting from. Makes the timescale of the prescriptive arc explicit so that institution-builders entering the work know what shape it has to take.
concepts.plain: Institutions that keep hard knowledge alive take decades or centuries to build, so rebuilding them is a job for generations.

concepts.label: Capture taxonomy (substrate × source × target asymmetry)
concepts.summary: The unified treatment of capture across the book. Capture is one mechanism — tuning a selection-design surface against the desideratum it was supposed to serve — operating across three axes: substrate (which selection-design surface is captured), source (external adversary / institution's own operating logic / composite), and target asymmetry (recovery dynamics determined by the substrate). Two cross-cutting principles: consumer-key captures are harder to recover from than surface captures; training-objective capture is uniquely bad because it self-reinforces across model generations. Composition rule: self-capture creates the gradient external capture rides, so composite capture is the empirically dominant mode.
concepts.plain: Anything that filters what people see or learn can be turned against its purpose; the questions are which filter, by whom, and how fixable.

concepts.label: Consumer-key vs. surface capture
concepts.summary: A cross-cutting principle the capture-taxonomy makes visible. Captures of substrates that install decoding-key machinery in consumers (receiver-training, training-corpus, training-objective) are harder to recover from than captures of substrates that only shape the surface a consumer encounters (gate-criteria, option-space, deployment-configuration, preservation-archive). The first kind damages the consumer; the second damages only the substrate. Generalizes Ch 8's capture-asymmetry between training and preservation into a substrate-level principle that applies wherever an LLM corpus, an LLM objective, or an institutional curriculum is the captured surface.
concepts.plain: Rigging what people are taught does deeper, longer-lasting damage than rigging what they are shown, because you cannot easily unteach a person.

passages.section: Axis 1: which substrate is captured, and how it recovers

concepts.label: LLM as collapsed selection-design moment
concepts.summary: An LLM is the first node in the book's information pipeline that owns gate + option-space + content-generator + training-corpus + training-objective + deployment-configuration + pricing-tier, all collapsed into one design moment owned by one party. Where a Ch 10 social-media platform owns two or three selection-design surfaces, an LLM owner owns five-to-seven. The structural concentration is what makes the LLM the limit case for the book's political-economy argument: every concern about ownership of selection design applies with sharper force.
aliases: LLM as new kind of node
concepts.plain: With an AI chatbot, one company picks what it learned from, what it was rewarded for, how it is configured, and also writes the answer.

concepts.label: Decompression on demand
concepts.summary: An LLM, used as a faithful expansion service, can take a compressed claim or a complex source and re-expand it into a form pre-loaded with the preconditions a receiver needs to decode it. This is the first structural way out of the fixed receiver-budget constraint the book has named: the receiver's budget has not changed, but the amount of complex form they can engage per unit of budget has gone up, because the LLM is paying the decompression cost. Conditional on faithfulness — a hallucinating LLM supplies plausible-but-wrong outer messages, which is worse than no outer message at all.
concepts.plain: An AI can unpack a dense paper into an explanation fitted to what you already know, as long as it stays faithful to the source.

concepts.label: Compressed form becoming authoritative
concepts.summary: The inverse failure mode of decompression-on-demand: at scale, the LLM-compressed summary of a source substitutes for the source itself in the network's working memory, with the LLM's authority backing the compressed version. The original is technically still there; nobody reads it. The summary is technically not the original; everybody reads it. Compression becomes substitution rather than abstraction — the receiver does not in practice go back and check, because the compressed form arrived with epistemic credentials no prior compression had.
concepts.plain: When an AI summary is treated as the answer, people stop reading the original, and the summary quietly takes its place.

passages.section: The summary that replaces the source

concepts.label: Corpus capture
concepts.summary: Capture of an LLM by selection of the training corpus. The most upstream version of capture in an LLM: choosing what data the model was fitted to (what included, in what proportions, with what filtering) tilts every output regardless of how careful the runtime gate is. A captured corpus produces a captured outer message — every output is decoded by receivers using the very preconditions the corpus installed. The capture-taxonomy interlude places it alongside the other flavors of capture.
concepts.plain: An AI trained on a lopsided selection of text gives lopsided answers, however carefully it is handled afterward.

passages.section: Axis 1: which substrate is captured, and how it recovers

concepts.label: Objective capture
concepts.summary: Capture of an LLM by the training objective (loss function, RLHF reward signal). A captured objective produces outputs that score well on the captured proxy and badly on whatever the actual desideratum was. Uniquely bad in the capture-taxonomy because it self-reinforces across model generations — the model's outputs go on to influence what data is generated downstream (the internet itself), which then feeds the next model's training corpus, baking the captured objective's effects across model generations. The substrate with the worst recovery dynamics in the book.
concepts.plain: An AI rewarded for pleasing people learns to please rather than to be right, and its output then feeds the next AI's training.

passages.section: Axis 1: which substrate is captured, and how it recovers

concepts.label: Deployment capture
concepts.summary: Capture of an LLM at inference time through system prompts, fine-tunes, distillations, refusal policies, and tool-use constraints. The cheapest of the LLM capture surfaces because it changes nothing about the model — same weights, used differently per request — and per the capture-taxonomy a surface capture rather than a consumer-key capture. Most opaque in practice because the configurations are typically not published and can change silently between requests.
concepts.plain: The company running an AI can change how it answers with hidden instructions, without retraining it and without users seeing the change.

passages.section: Axis 1: which substrate is captured, and how it recovers

concepts.label: Capture asymmetry (training vs. preservation)
concepts.summary: Under institutional capture, the training half does more damage and recovers more slowly than the preservation half. A captured preservation institution holds a tuned version of the complex form — in principle re-discoverable from external evidence and alternative archives. A captured training institution tunes the receivers themselves, and trained perceptual machinery cannot be easily un-trained: subsequent un-captured preservation has to work against a re-tuned readership that decodes incoming evidence through the installed key. The asymmetry decides which half a network has to defend first when the institution is under pressure. Per the capture-taxonomy this is the special case of the more general consumer-key-vs-surface principle.
concepts.plain: A corrupted library can be rebuilt from other sources, but people trained to read wrongly are slow to retrain, so corrupted teaching is usually worse.

passages.section: Axis 1: which substrate is captured, and how it recovers

concepts.label: Differential decay rates (preservation vs. training)
concepts.summary: Preservation institutions degrade slowly — archives and journals can run on inertia for decades with the loss mostly invisible until someone tries to use the form. Training institutions degrade within a generation — every cohort needs to be carried fresh, and once the producers of versatile experts stop producing, supply runs out within a working lifetime. Together with the capture asymmetry, this makes training the more time-sensitive function to defend even though preservation is what the institution rhetorically advertises.
concepts.plain: A neglected library can sit intact for decades, but skilled people must be trained fresh every generation, so teaching fails first.

passages.section: What this means for the modern environment

concepts.label: Memetic fitness
concepts.summary: The local fitness criteria at each selection gate: emotional valence, identity reinforcement, status, action affordance, novelty, controversy. None coordinated, none particularly interested in truth-preservation.
concepts.plain: What gets passed along is whatever stirs feeling, flatters a group, or gives people something to do, and being true is not on that list.

concepts.label: Transferable preconditions
concepts.summary: Field-general capacities (statistical literacy, critical reading, the disposition to look for evidence) that help receivers engage with many domains. The outline's first-pass answer for what makes a bridge node; refined in bridge-nodes-and-versatile-expertise into the paired skill alongside depth rather than the bridge itself.
concepts.plain: General skills like reading statistics and asking for evidence help in every subject, but alone they cannot carry expert knowledge between fields.

concepts.label: Versatile expertise
concepts.summary: Deep specialist expertise paired with metacognitive flexibility — the second-order capacity to recognize structural analogies across domains, suspend one's primary paradigm, and treat one's own frame as one option rather than the substrate of reality. The bridge-node mechanism: depth is what gets a bridge admitted as a peer on either side; flexibility is what lets it see and translate the structural analogy that crosses. Refines the outline's 'transferable preconditions' answer into the paired-skill form.
concepts.plain: The people who can carry hard ideas between fields are deep specialists who also know their own way of seeing is only one of several.

concepts.label: The curse of expertise
concepts.summary: Four cognitive failure modes of deep specialization without paired metacognitive flexibility: paradigm lock-in (can't entertain other frames), overconfidence in cross-application (over-extends mastery), perceptual filtering (screens out information that doesn't fit), conceptual rigidity (can't reframe a problem). Together these are the cognitive substrate of polarization-via-distrust — same mechanism, vocabulary at the individual level instead of the network level.
concepts.plain: Knowing one field very deeply can make it harder to see, or take seriously, anything that does not fit that field's way of thinking.

concepts.label: The abyss
concepts.summary: The possibility-space of a sufficiently complex field — every move, question, or direction it could go — when that space outgrows any traverser's budget, so that no one, expert or machine, can navigate or even fully perceive it. It takes real competence in a field just to see that its abyss is there; novices mistake the field for something finite. Two load-bearing roles in the book: 'expertise is a compression of the abyss' (chunking and heuristics are a lossy map of a territory too large to traverse), which ties compression to the receiver-budget constraint; and the experiential complement of the curse of expertise — the curse is depth that hasn't seen the abyss, the bridge node is depth that has. Distinct from optionality-vs-access, which is the approachability of a finite, masterable artifact: the artifact is a map, the abyss is the territory.
concepts.plain: Any rich field holds far more possible paths than anyone could ever explore, and you only see that once you are good at it.

passages.section: What the curve is, and what it isn't
The summary that replaces the source

concepts.label: Handle-ability
concepts.summary: Proposed alternative to 'complexity' as the real gating variable: how many existing mental models an idea plugs into, how much emotional or identity content it carries, whether it tells the receiver what to do. Selection-side property.
concepts.plain: Ideas spread when they are easy to grab: they fit what people already think, stir a feeling, and say what to do.

concepts.label: Meme ecosystem competition
concepts.summary: Memes don't propagate in isolation — a meme's infection and decay rates are functions of the other memes already competing for the same attention. Fitness is relative to the current population, not an intrinsic property. (Catalog gap flagged by the epidemiological-virality extraction.)
concepts.plain: How far an idea spreads depends on what else is competing for people's attention at the same moment.

concepts.label: Neutral drift baseline (Yule process)
concepts.summary: The null model for spread: what propagation looks like with no selection at all — random copying plus rich-get-richer accumulation. Most meme variants follow it. Selection is what you detect as departure from this baseline. (Catalog gap flagged by the info-evolution extraction.)
concepts.plain: Even if nobody preferred any version of an idea, random copying alone would make a few versions hugely popular and leave most obscure.

concepts.label: Replicator ontology
concepts.summary: The assumption that culture comes in discrete, copyable units (memes as replicators, analogous to genes). The load-bearing premise of memetics — and the one its critics attack hardest, arguing cultural transmission is reconstructive, not copy-based. (Catalog gap flagged by the memetics-critique extraction.)
concepts.plain: Calling ideas "memes" quietly assumes they are separate units copied like genes, and critics argue people rebuild ideas instead of copying them.

concepts.label: Paradox of virality
concepts.summary: What spreads is not what people endorse. Across the political spectrum, people report they do not want high-arousal negative content to go viral — yet it does. The gap implicates the selection gate (especially algorithmic amplification), not receiver preference. (Catalog gap flagged by the psychology-of-virality extraction.)
concepts.plain: Most people say they do not want angry, alarming posts to go viral, and those posts go viral anyway.

passages.section: The strongest objection: people are not that gullible

concepts.label: Superspreader dynamics
concepts.summary: A small number of high-degree nodes drive a disproportionate share of total spread — a network-structure effect with no offline equivalent at the same scale. Distinct from manipulation surface: it's about who is positioned to amplify, not what can be exploited. (Catalog gap flagged by the psychology-of-virality extraction.)
concepts.plain: A tiny number of very well-connected accounts do most of the spreading, something that was impossible before networks got this big.

concepts.label: Algorithm as selection engine
concepts.summary: Recommendation algorithms are not lossy transport — they are selection gates with adjustable weights. They make 'who tunes the gates' a literal, operational question, and turn the selection criteria of a few companies into the selection criteria of everyone. (Catalog gap flagged by the psychology-of-virality extraction.)
concepts.plain: A feed's ranking software is a filter with dials that someone sets, and it decides what millions of people see.

passages.section: Three things the medium does to a gate
The strongest objection: people are not that gullible

concepts.label: Epistemic vigilance (mental immune systems)
concepts.summary: The Sperberian-tradition construct for the cognitive defenses humans have evolved to screen incoming information for plausibility and source reliability — 'mental immune systems' in the popular framing. Mercier extends and refines the term as *open vigilance* (see open-vigilance concept) to mark that the system is paired with openness rather than being a one-sided defense layer over a credulous default. The catalog keeps both entries because earlier book chapters used 'epistemic vigilance' before the Mercier extraction sharpened it.
concepts.plain: People come equipped with mental defenses that check whether a claim is plausible and whether its source can be trusted.

passages.section: The strongest objection: people are not that gullible

concepts.label: Open vigilance (Mercier's paired construct)
concepts.summary: Mercier's refinement of Sperber's epistemic-vigilance term. The system is paired: humans are simultaneously *open to* useful information and *vigilant against* unreliable sources, with the two faces evolving hand-in-hand as communication became broader and more powerful. The earlier 'epistemic vigilance' label flattens this into a one-sided defense construct, which is what the catalog had until the Mercier extraction surfaced the paired reading. Two named sub-mechanisms: *plausibility checking* (does the message fit pre-existing beliefs?) and *reasoning* (do supporting arguments resonate?). Calibration is asymmetric: more errors of omission (not trusting when we should) than of commission (trusting when we shouldn't) — vigilance is conservative-leaning, not credulous-leaning.
concepts.plain: People are both open to useful information and wary of unreliable sources, and their mistakes lean toward doubting too much.

passages.section: The strongest objection: people are not that gullible

concepts.label: Reflective vs. intuitive belief (Sperber's split)
concepts.summary: Dan Sperber's distinction between two ways a person can hold a belief. *Intuitive beliefs* are integrated with one's other beliefs and freely drive inferences and action — they are load-bearing. *Reflective beliefs* are held propositionally without integration — verbal, contextual, often shared as identity-signals or coalition-markers, but inert with respect to action. The split underwrites Mercier's reading of the paradox-of-virality: 'most false rumors are held reflectively, for they would have much more serious consequences if they were held intuitively.' Conspiracy theories, witches' confessions, absurd flattery, and political-affiliation claims are typically reflective. Explains the share/endorse gap without needing a strong gate-amplification story — the gap is by design at the cognitive layer.
concepts.plain: Some beliefs steer what you actually do, while others you only say or share and never act on.

concepts.label: Justification market (behavior→belief arrow)
concepts.summary: Mercier's reframe of the causal arrow between content consumption and behavior. The naive story (and the book's implicit Part-IV-supply-side framing): content shapes belief, belief drives behavior. Mercier's reversal: behavior is determined upstream (by group identity, in-group commitments, status concerns, material interest); receivers then demand-side select for content that *justifies* the already-decided behavior. The market for false beliefs is therefore downstream of action-already-chosen, and what looks like 'mass persuasion installing beliefs' is more often suppliers of justifications meeting receivers' pre-existing demand. The Trump-supporter finding (corrections accepted, behavior unchanged) is the diagnostic anchor: when corrections land and behavior doesn't move, the belief was never load-bearing for the behavior.
concepts.plain: People often decide what to do first and then go looking for beliefs that make the decision feel right.

concepts.label: The three-layer message (frame / outer / inner)
concepts.summary: Hofstadter's anatomy of any message (Gödel, Escher, Bach, Ch VI): the frame message ('I am a message, decode me'), the outer message (the decoding mechanism the receiver must already hold — implicit, carried by the medium), and the inner message (the meaning the sender intended). The book adapts it: each pipeline re-encoding can strip a layer independently, and the outer message is what the book calls preconditions.
concepts.plain: Every message has three parts: a sign that it is a message, the know-how needed to read it, and the content itself.

passages.section: What a message is made of

concepts.label: Network segmentation
concepts.summary: The fracturing of a network into sub-groups along the seams of its binding myth's interpretive latitude. The segments affirm the same myth while decoding it differently, so the network is superficially unified and structurally fragmented at once. Distinct from echo chambers vs. bubbles: this is the process that produces those structures.
concepts.plain: A huge group can repeat the same slogan while its subgroups each mean something different by it, so it is already several groups underneath.

passages.section: The diagnosis: segmentation is the default

concepts.label: Truth-compression regimes (preservation / inversion / orthogonality)
concepts.summary: The three things compression can do to a claim's truth value, set by the gap between the idea's decoding key and the key the receiver supplies: preservation (keys close — a low-resolution true image), inversion (keys opposed — a true claim decoded into a false belief), and orthogonality (the claim is read as an identity flag, its truth value intact but no longer the operative axis). The selection gate decides which regime a compressed variant lands in.
concepts.plain: A shortened claim can stay roughly true, flip into something false, or turn into a team badge, depending on how the listener reads it.

passages.section: Three things compression can do to truth
Truth value isn't in the claim

concepts.label: Option space
concepts.summary: The set of forms an idea can take at a given pipeline stage — the menu selection picks from. Transport generates candidate variants; the medium bounds which of them are viable; selection ranks what remains. Selection never enlarges the option space, it only chooses within it, which is why the medium that writes the menu is the higher-leverage and less visible surface.
concepts.plain: Before anyone chooses which version of an idea to pass on, the format has already decided which versions can exist at all.

passages.section: Three things the medium does to a gate

concepts.label: Technology vs. medium
concepts.summary: Postman's distinction between a technology — the machine or tool itself — and a medium — the social and intellectual environment that grows up around how the technology is used. The book's 'medium' always means the latter: not the device but the environment of capacities, gate-criteria, and cultivated wants it produces. The same technology can host different media, which guards against blaming the hardware for what is really a pattern of use.
concepts.plain: A machine is one thing; the habits, rewards and expectations that grow up around using it are another, and those are what shape us.

passages.section: The medium is not the pipe

concepts.label: Pseudo-context
concepts.summary: Postman's term for a structure invented to give decontextualized information the appearance of a use it does not really have. The information may be true and accurately measured, but it has been stripped of the context that connected it to action; pseudo-context — the news quiz, trivia, conversation-fodder — papers over the gap. Distinct from manufactured content, which never measured anything: pseudo-context is real information made idle.
concepts.plain: Trivia, news quizzes and factoid videos give true facts a pretend use after the real use has been stripped away.

concepts.label: The Orwell/Huxley axis
concepts.summary: Postman's framing of two opposite failure modes for an information ecosystem. The Orwell mode: control by inflicted pain — censorship, surveillance, information withheld. The Huxley mode: control by inflicted pleasure — truth not concealed but drowned in a sea of engaging irrelevance. The book's diagnosis sits squarely in the Huxley mode: the modern failure is abundance optimized for engagement, not scarcity enforced by a censor.
concepts.plain: A society can lose the truth by having it banned, or by having it buried under endless entertainment, and the second is harder to fight.

passages.section: The Orwell mode and the Huxley mode

concepts.label: False consensus among rational agents
concepts.summary: O'Connor & Weatherall's central result: a community of agents who each update on evidence correctly — perfect Bayesians, no irrationality, no gullibility — can still converge on a false belief. False consensus is a property of network structure and the way evidence propagates, not of individual error. It undercuts any diagnosis that locates the problem solely in receivers being careless or stupid.
concepts.plain: A group of people who each reason carefully and honestly can still end up agreeing on something false, because of how evidence reaches them.

passages.section: The strongest objection: people are not that gullible

concepts.label: Credibility weighting
concepts.summary: The practice — rational and unavoidable — of weighting a piece of evidence by how much the receiver trusts its source. In O'Connor & Weatherall's models this is the core mechanism of social belief: no one can verify everything first-hand, so trust in sources does the work. It is also the seam propaganda exploits — manufacture or buy credibility and the weighting carries false evidence as readily as true.
concepts.plain: Nobody can check everything personally, so we all judge claims partly by how much we trust whoever is telling us.

passages.section: The strongest objection: people are not that gullible

concepts.label: Conformity
concepts.summary: The adoption of a belief because one's peers hold it, rather than on the evidence for it. Distinct from the content-side criteria of memetic fitness: conformity weights the social fact of agreement itself. In O'Connor & Weatherall's models conformity pressure can lock a community onto a belief — true or false — and insulate it from correcting evidence.
concepts.plain: People often take up a belief because the people around them hold it, whatever the evidence says.

passages.section: The strongest objection: people are not that gullible

concepts.label: Polarization via distrust
concepts.summary: A self-reinforcing loop formalized by O'Connor & Weatherall: when agents discount evidence from sources they distrust, communities that begin with mild disagreement diverge — each side discounts the other's findings, beliefs pull apart, and the divergence deepens the distrust that drove it. Polarization here needs no irrationality and no misinformation; rational trust-weighting plus an initial difference is enough.
concepts.plain: Two groups that start slightly apart can drift far apart just by sensibly giving less weight to evidence from people they trust less.

concepts.label: The Zollman effect
concepts.summary: The counterintuitive result (Kevin Zollman, central to O'Connor & Weatherall's account) that increasing a community's connectivity can reduce the accuracy of its beliefs: densely connected agents see each other's preliminary, noisy results too quickly and converge prematurely on whichever answer took an early lead. More communication is not monotonically better — there is an optimum. Bears directly on the Part IV integration question.
concepts.plain: Wiring a group together more tightly can make it less accurate, because everyone hears early, shaky results and settles on an answer too soon.

concepts.label: Truth generators (reality vs. agreement)
concepts.summary: The carving that disciplines the three-realities frame: objective truths are generated by reality (the pipeline can garble the claim but cannot touch the fact); intersubjective truths are generated by the network's agreement — kept as truths, in Harari's terms, because the generator differs, not the truth-ness. Carves per-claim, not per-artifact: a myth can be based in reality too, and mixed bundles (founding stories, astrology) split along the generator line. Every intersubjective truth also casts an objective shadow — that the agreement holds is an ordinary objective fact about the network — and keeping a truth apart from its shadow is what keeps reporting-on-a-constitution distinct from participating-in-one.
concepts.plain: Two statements can both be true while one is made true by the world and the other only by people continuing to agree.

concepts.label: Constitutive regimes (convergent / divergent / hollow)
concepts.summary: What 5c's truth-regimes become when the cargo's generator is the agreement itself: convergent constitution (decodes compose into one determinate agreement — most money and law, most of the time), divergent constitution (decodes pool into camps affirming the same words as different agreements — segmentation read one level up, the truth coming apart), and hollow constitution (symbolic affirmation detaches from the constituting behavior — everyone still calls it money, nobody holds it). The failure axis rotates from error to spread-and-substance: an intersubjective truth cannot be inverted, but it can split or empty. Carries the same two-plus-one suspicion as 5c's regimes, inherited knowingly.
concepts.plain: A shared agreement like money or law can hold together, split into rival versions, or survive in words only while people stop acting on it.

concepts.label: Reification
concepts.summary: Treating a made thing as a found thing: an intersubjective truth processed as if objective — 'money just is valuable,' 'the market decided,' 'the law is the law.' The mirror image of 5c's orthogonality migration (an objective claim processed as intersubjective). The two migrations do opposite damage: orthogonality makes an answerable claim unanswerable; reification makes a renegotiable arrangement look unrenegotiable — which is the camouflage a captured generator wants most, since an agreement that reads as a law of nature has a generator nobody audits. De-reification is therefore a political act, and Ch 10's job description in one word.
aliases: agreement wearing the costume of nature
concepts.plain: People forget that money, markets and laws are arrangements humans made and could remake, and start treating them like facts of nature.

passages.section: Capture, when there is no truth to tune against

concepts.label: Framework (a medium for thought)
concepts.summary: Any human-made structure one thinks inside: a language, notation, metaphor, classification, model, metric, tool or organization. The book treats a framework as a medium for thought: selection performed once, in advance, on what its users will find easy to notice, record and say. It is the medium argument moved one step upstream, to the hop from the world to a measurement and to the inside of a single head before anything is sent. A framework does four things: decides what can be recorded (capacity / legibility), makes some operations cheap and others laborious (cost asymmetry), supplies the default, and feeds back on the world when acted on. Named independently by a dozen fields (linguistic relativity, theory-ladenness, framing, legibility, Goodhart, performativity, Conway, inductive bias). Provisional; rests on the frameworks report.

passages.section: A framework is a medium you think in
What a framework does to a thought

concepts.plain: Any structure people build to think with, such as a language, a form, a metric or a model, quietly shapes what they find easy to think.

concepts.label: Cost asymmetry
concepts.summary: Inside a framework some operations are cheap and others laborious, and over time people mostly do what is cheap. Leibniz's dy/dx encodes the chain rule in its symbols where Newton's dots do not; a slide format makes bullet hierarchies cheap and sustained argument costly; place-value numerals make long division routine. The working part of framework pricing, and the same trade Ch 4 finds in every designed artifact (optionality vs access): what is easy to reach was paid for with what is hard to reach.

passages.section: What a framework does to a thought
What the curve is, and what it isn't

concepts.plain: Inside any tool or system of notation, some things take one step and others take fifty, and people mostly do the one-step things.

concepts.label: Defaults
concepts.summary: The unmarked option a framework supplies when nothing is chosen: a reference point, a category, a prompt template, a pre-ticked box. Framing studies show defaults steer choices even when the alternatives are logically equivalent. The report's one-line statement of the whole strand: the framework sets the default, and defaults drive outcomes. The cheapest item on the framework's price list, and the quietest place to steer.

passages.section: What a framework does to a thought

concepts.plain: Whatever a system gives you when you make no choice is what most people end up with, so whoever sets the default sets the outcome.

concepts.label: Influence, not imprisonment
concepts.summary: The graded-effects finding: wherever the strong claim (a framework fixes what its users can think) has been tested hard, it has failed; what survives is a weak but measurable bias toward whatever the framework makes easy, visible or rewarded. Pirahã speakers match exact quantities without number words; the Russian-blues advantage vanishes under verbal interference; chess experts escape the familiar pattern when it is a blunder; Boroditsky's time-metaphor result failed replication. The book takes it as a correction to its own 'never forms' in 5b: rarely forms. Changes the remedy (a price can be paid; a wall must be torn down). Open worry: a price nobody pays for a generation may harden into lock-in.

passages.section: The price list, not the wall

concepts.plain: The tools you think with tilt your thinking in measurable ways, but careful testing shows they do not trap it.

concepts.label: Linguistic relativity
concepts.summary: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis: the language one speaks influences habitual thought. The strong (determinist) form is rejected; the weak form holds in specific domains with modest effects: color (Winawer et al. 2007, Russian blues, an 'online' effect removed by verbal interference), space (Levinson's Guugu Yimithirr absolute-frame results, still debated), number (Frank et al. 2008, Pirahã: number words as cognitive technology). Specific findings are fragile: Boroditsky's 2001 time-metaphor result failed six replications. The oldest and best-tested case of a framework biasing the thinking done inside it, and the clearest evidence for influence, not imprisonment.

passages.section: The price list, not the wall
A framework is a medium you think in

concepts.plain: The language you speak nudges what you notice and remember, but it does not decide what you are able to think.

concepts.label: Notation as a tool of thought
concepts.summary: Iverson's 1979 Turing lecture: notation is a tool of thought, and an effective one must allow convenient expression of the notions that arise in later analysis and generalization as well as the first ones. Leibniz's dy/dx vs Newton's dots; place-value vs Roman numerals; programming languages (Graham's Blub paradox). A clean instance of cost asymmetry, and the hopeful case: a good notation lets a finite mind hold more. Subject to lock-in. Historical-case support; little experimental work.
aliases: notation as a tool of thought

passages.section: What a framework does to a thought
What the curve is, and what it isn't

concepts.plain: The symbols you write a problem in decide which steps are easy, so a better notation puts harder thoughts within reach.

concepts.label: Framing effect
concepts.summary: Tversky and Kahneman (Science, 1981): logically equivalent descriptions produce different choices. In the disease problem 72% chose the certain program under a lives-saved description and 78% chose the risky program under a lives-lost description of identical outcomes. Robustly replicated (Many Labs: 31 of 36 samples; a 47-country 2020 survey), smaller than the original. Goffman's frame analysis is the sociological ancestor. The cleanest proof that a framework biases thought with nothing hidden or false, and a close cousin of the book's key-fit account of truth under compression: same inner message, different frame, different decode.

passages.section: What a framework does to a thought

concepts.plain: Describe the same facts in two different ways and people will make two different choices.

concepts.label: Conceptual metaphor
concepts.summary: Lakoff and Johnson (Metaphors We Live By, 1980): abstract domains are structured by metaphors from concrete ones (ARGUMENT IS WAR, TIME IS MONEY), and the metaphor shapes inference. Best-known test: Thibodeau and Boroditsky (2011), crime as beast vs virus; contested by Steen et al. (2014) on effect size and coding, reproduced in a German replication (2016); depends on early placement and prior attitudes. Evidence mixed. For the book a metaphor is a compact framework that survives compression when the qualifications do not, which is why it does so much work in the bridge zone. McLuhan's 'the medium is the message' is the media-scale sibling.

passages.section: A framework is a medium you think in

concepts.plain: The comparison you use to describe a problem quietly suggests which solutions make sense.

concepts.label: Theory-ladenness and paradigms
concepts.summary: Hanson (1958): what a scientist sees depends on the conceptual background brought to the observation. Kuhn (1962) extends it to communities: a paradigm defines which puzzles are legitimate and sets anomalies aside until crisis. Duhem-Quine: evidence tests a bundle, so the framework decides what gets blamed (Ptolemaic epicycles). Foucault's episteme is the era-wide version. Philosophical, with strong historical-case support. In the book's vocabulary a paradigm is a specialist community's shared decoding key (outer message), which is why findings cross between fields badly and why deep training can blind as well as equip.

passages.section: A framework is a medium you think in

concepts.plain: What an expert sees when looking at evidence depends on the theory they already hold.

concepts.label: Einstellung effect
concepts.summary: A known solution method blocks the search for better ones (Luchins's water jars, 1942); functional fixedness (Duncker's candle problem) is the sibling. Bilalić, McLeod and Gobet (2008): chess experts who had found a familiar solution reported searching for a better one while their eye movements kept returning to the familiar pattern. Boundary condition (Sheridan and Reingold, 2013): when the familiar move was an outright blunder, all experts avoided it. Robust. A framework installed by practice rather than design: a learned method acting as an attention-capturing default. The lab-scale cousin of the curse of expertise.

passages.section: The price list, not the wall

concepts.plain: Once you know one way to solve a problem, that way keeps pulling your attention back and hides better ones.

concepts.label: Law of the instrument
concepts.summary: Maslow (1966): 'it is tempting, if the only tool you have is a hammer, to treat everything as if it were a nail' (also Kaplan, 1964). Tools define the problems seen. The streetlight effect is its measurement cousin: people search where it is easy to look. Anecdotal and observational support. The everyday face of framework pricing: the tool you own is the cheap option. Trained into a person it becomes Einstellung and the curse of expertise; built into an institution's instruments it becomes legibility.

passages.section: A framework is a medium you think in

concepts.plain: People reach for the tool they already have, and then see every problem as one that tool can fix.

concepts.label: Inductive bias
concepts.summary: Every learning algorithm needs assumptions beyond the data to generalize at all: convolutions assume locality and translation invariance, linear models additivity, tokenizers fix the units a language model reasons over (irregular chunking of digits makes arithmetic harder, a direct analogue of Roman numerals). The one field where framework bias is treated as unavoidable and designed deliberately rather than as an error. The same field shows how fast implicit frameworks (benchmarks, prompt templates) shape research and output. Necessary, not a defect: the aim is to choose biases deliberately and test against them.

passages.section: The clearest case is a machine

concepts.plain: A system that learns from examples has to make assumptions that go beyond those examples, and the assumptions shape everything it concludes.

concepts.label: The map is not the territory
concepts.summary: Korzybski (1933): the representation is not the thing represented; reification is treating an abstraction as concrete. Box: all models are wrong (1976), but some are useful (1979). Taleb's ludic fallacy: treating real-world uncertainty as if it had the tidy structure of games. Model risk is the regulatory name for losses from flawed or misapplied models. A warning, not a mechanism. The book adds two things: a map drawn for a budget-limited reader is unavoidable (the abyss is the territory), so the goal is to remember what was left out; and maps get acted on, at which point the territory starts changing (framework feedback).
aliases: the map is not the territory

passages.section: When the map starts moving the territory
What the curve is, and what it isn't

concepts.plain: A model or a summary is a simplified picture of something, and trouble starts when people forget what the picture left out.

concepts.label: Legibility
concepts.summary: James C. Scott (Seeing Like a State, 1998): the state's effort 'to make a society legible, to arrange the population in ways that simplified the classic state functions of taxation, conscription, and prevention of rebellion.' State simplifications are 'rather like abridged maps', but maps that, 'when allied with state power, would enable much of the reality they depicted to be remade.' What the framework cannot record drops out of reasoning (the foresters saw saleable volume; underbrush, soil biota and diversity lay 'outside the brackets'). For the book this is the framework at the pipeline's first hop (the Out There to Raw Data): the medium of the measurement gate, and the entry point for torque and feedback. Historical case studies.

passages.section: What a framework does to a thought
When the map starts moving the territory

concepts.plain: To manage something large, you first simplify it into what can be written down, and whatever cannot be written down stops counting.

concepts.label: Classification torque
concepts.summary: Bowker and Star (Sorting Things Out, 1999): classification systems are infrastructure, invisible when they work and consequential for everyone sorted by them. Torque names 'a twisting of time lines that pull at each other', a mismatch in which 'Lives are twisted, even torn, in the attempt to force the one into the other.' 'Politically and socially charged agendas are often first presented as purely technical and they are difficult even to see.' Cases: apartheid race classification, the ICD. What legibility costs the people made legible; a category that reads as nature is one nobody audits (reification). Historical and ethnographic.

passages.section: A framework is a medium you think in
Bureaucracy is downstream of the myth

concepts.plain: When official categories do not fit the people sorted into them, the categories hold and the people are the ones who bend.

concepts.label: Goodhart's law
concepts.summary: Goodhart (1975): 'Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.' The aphorism 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure' is Strathern's 1997 generalization. Campbell's law (1979): the more a quantitative social indicator is used for decision-making, the more subject it is to corruption pressures and the more it distorts the processes it monitors. Target substitution: effort flows to the measure rather than what it stood for. Widely documented. For the book, the prior art for Ch 10's 'engagement is a proxy for revenue, dressed up as a proxy for user benefit', and for objective capture in Ch 11. Framework feedback in its commonest form.
aliases: when a measure becomes a target

passages.section: When the map starts moving the territory
The clearest case is a machine

concepts.plain: Once people are rewarded for hitting a number, they find ways to hit it that no longer deliver what the number was meant to track.

concepts.label: Performativity
concepts.summary: MacKenzie (An Engine, Not a Camera, 2006): financial models are engines that shape markets, not cameras that record them. Barnesian performativity: using a model makes reality more like the model (Black-Scholes-Merton, 1976 to summer 1987). Counterperformativity: use makes reality less like it (the post-1987 skew). MacKenzie denies the crude version: not any arbitrary formula could have made itself true, and consistency with performativity does not prove it. Compelling for options; general scope debated. The best-documented case of framework feedback, and the outside literature's name for what the book calls constitutive transmission; pairs with Soros's reflexivity and Hacking's looping effects.

passages.section: When the map starts moving the territory
The pipeline is wired into its own cargo

concepts.plain: A model that enough people use to make decisions can stop merely describing the world and start pushing the world toward itself.

concepts.label: Looping effects
concepts.summary: Hacking ('making up people'; The Social Construction of What?): human kinds differ from natural kinds because the people classified respond to their classification, which changes the people and therefore the category. Philosophical/historical. Framework feedback applied to the sorting of human beings; sits beside torque (what categories do to lives) and performativity (what models do to markets). The intersubjective-truth note flags Hacking as owed a closer reading for the self-fulfilling-loop material.

passages.section: When the map starts moving the territory

concepts.plain: People who are put in a category react to being put there, and their reaction changes what the category contains.

concepts.label: Conway's law
concepts.summary: Conway (1968): systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that design them (the 'mirroring hypothesis'). MacCormack, Rusnak and Baldwin (2012): in matched pairs of products with the same function, the product from the loosely coupled organization was significantly more modular in every pair. Colfer and Baldwin (2016), 142 studies: 70% strong support, 22% partial, 8% none; most descriptive studies of open collaborative projects did not support it. Reversible on purpose (the inverse Conway maneuver). An org chart as a framework: talking to the next desk is cheap, talking across departments is expensive, and the product takes that shape.

passages.section: A framework is a medium you think in

concepts.plain: The things an organization builds end up shaped like the organization's own internal lines of communication.

concepts.label: Path dependence and lock-in
concepts.summary: David (1985), Arthur (1989): early, sometimes arbitrary choices get entrenched by network effects, training, tooling, standards and sunk investment, so a framework survives after its fit has declined (fluxional notation at Cambridge, arguably QWERTY, the DSM's continued use). The concept is accepted; the QWERTY example is disputed (Liebowitz and Margolis: evidence for Dvorak's superiority is 'scant and suspect'; only third-degree path dependence implies a remediable inefficiency). The Overton window is the political version. Lock-in is what turns a framework's price list into something closer to a wall over time.
concepts.plain: An early choice, even an arbitrary one, can become nearly impossible to change once everyone has built their habits around it.

concepts.label: Framework rotation
concepts.summary: The countermeasure family: single frameworks fail silently; disagreement between several exposes the shape of each. Use several models/notations and look for disagreement (ensembles, triangulation); report results across framings (prompt-format ranges; gains and losses; absolute and relative risk); separate measures from targets and rotate indicators; change the notation when the problem changes; red-team the categories, not just the conclusions; treat models as engines and expect feedback; design organizations for the architecture wanted; seek out-of-framework input (pre-mortems, outsider review); keep Box's maxim operational. The framework strand's answer and the book's larger one in miniature: versatile expertise is rotation practiced by one person; survivable-polarization design is rotation built into an institution.
concepts.plain: The way to see how one way of looking is bending your view is to look a second way and compare.
